title: America's Teahouse Boom Meets India's Chai Heritage as Tea Goes Mainstream
excerpt: Chinese tea chains and late-night teahouses are driving a tea revolution across US cities, creating new space for India's deep chai traditions.
body:
• Chinese tea chains Heytea, Teapulse, and Mixue are rapidly expanding across US cities, with Heytea now operating over 40 locations and opening its first overseas concept store in New York
  • Late-night teahouses are emerging as alcohol-free social spaces in cities like Los Angeles, driven by declining alcohol consumption among younger Americans
  • The trend creates new cultural space for India's chai traditions, with brands like Kolkata Chai Co bringing authentic desi chai to American consumers
  • Tea remains a "permissible indulgence" for budget-conscious consumers, with drinks priced between $2 and $8

Tea is having a moment in America — and it is a big one. A wave of Chinese tea chains is winning converts from coffee with fruit-infused brews and cheese foam toppings, while late-night teahouses in cities like Los Angeles are redefining nightlife without alcohol. For the Indian diaspora, the boom carries a familiar ring: a country that consumes over a billion kilograms of tea annually is watching its adopted home finally take the leaf seriously.

The Chinese Tea Chain Expansion

Heytea, Teapulse, and Mixue are leading the charge. Heytea, which operates more than 3,500 locations worldwide, opened its first overseas concept store — called a Teabar — on New York's Upper East Side on June 5. Lines stretched three blocks long on opening day, according to AllRecipes. The chain now has over 40 US locations across New York, California, Houston, Seattle, and Boston.

Teapulse is approaching 10 stores in New York and has plans to expand into 25 states. Mixue, with nearly 50,000 locations globally and a recent public listing, has six stores in New York and a similar number in California.

"Once we got in, I realized why there was that big wait. I'm not so much into tea, but I'm getting more into it now."

— Steven Sparling, New York customer, to Bloomberg

These chains are building on the bubble tea craze but pushing into new territory with premium ingredients — Chinese perfume lemons, osmanthus tea, guava-pear blends, and the now-iconic cheese foam topping that Heytea pioneered. Prices range from $2 at Mixue to about $8 for Heytea's matcha lattes. The brightly colored drinks are engineered for Instagram and TikTok, and the stores emphasize socializing over laptop work.

Late-Night Teahouses Replace the Bar

The trend extends well beyond chain stores. In Los Angeles, late-night teahouses — some hidden behind unmarked doors, some viral on TikTok, some requiring memberships — are popping up as alternatives to bars and clubs. The shift tracks a broader change in drinking habits: a 2023 Gallup study found that the number of Americans under 35 who drink alcohol dropped 10% over the past two decades.

Salanya Angel Inm opened Jai Tea Loft in Koreatown after years of feeling Los Angeles lacked late-night spaces not centered on alcohol. Lydia Lin co-founded Steep in Chinatown, seeking a place "peaceful enough that she could hear her friends while having a conversation," according to LA Times reporting. These teahouses are part of a growing demand for third spaces — gathering spots that are not home or work — centered on wellness and connection rather than drinking.

India's Chai Heritage in the Mix

For Indian Americans, the teahouse boom is both validating and, at times, frustrating. India's chai culture runs centuries deep — from the roadside chaiwallah simmering masala chai with fresh ginger and cardamom to the elaborate family tea rituals that vary by region, from Kolkata's adda culture to the Nilgiri hills. Yet in mainstream American cafes, "chai tea latte" has long flattened centuries of tradition into a cinnamon-sweetened afterthought — the name itself, translating to "tea tea latte," a persistent source of bewilderment for Indians.

That gap is narrowing. Kolkata Chai Co, founded in New York by Indian American siblings Ani and Ayan Sanyal, has built a devoted following serving authentic desi chai alongside Kolkata-style street food like egg rolls, samosas, and chaats. "There's still a lot of miseducation around what 'chai' really is," Ani Sanyal told The Better India. "But through social media posts and viral content, we have begun to reframe people's idea of chai." The cafe serves thousands of customers monthly and ships chai mixes across the US and Canada.

As American consumers develop more sophisticated palates for tea — exploring oolong, jasmine, and matcha — the path to appreciating India's masala chai, Darjeeling, Assam, and Nilgiri varieties gets shorter. Brands that bridge authentic Indian preparation with modern American presentation stand to benefit from a market that is finally paying attention.

Why Tea, Why Now

Economics play a role. David Portalatin, senior vice president at market research firm Circana, told Bloomberg that beverages remain a "permissible indulgence" for consumers otherwise cutting back on spending. Huy Do at Datassential attributed the trend to "little treat" culture — consumers bypassing larger purchases but willing to splurge on a sub-$10 drink that makes them feel good.

For the diaspora, the takeaway is straightforward: the country that shaped chai culture now has a growing market of Americans ready to take tea seriously. Whether that translates into mainstream appreciation for authentic Indian tea — or just more cheese foam — may depend on who brews the next cup.
